t: Persian, first written in the inscriptions of the Achaemenid kings in the 6th century BCE, has been spoken and written for some two and a half thousand years, in three stages known as Old, Middle and New Persian.

Reborn after the Arab conquest as New Persian, written in Arabic letters, it became from the 10th century the language of a great literature, from Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh to Rumi and Hafez, and of courts and learning from Anatolia to India.
The language of Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan today, it has changed so little since the 10th century that Persian speakers can still read the classical poets with ease.
dyk: Persian was the official language of the courts of British India until 1837, and words such as bazaar, caravan, pyjamas, paradise and checkmate, from shāh māt, “the king is helpless”, reached English from or through Persian.
ev: Darius I has his deeds carved in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian on the cliff of Behistun
Shapur I records his victories over Rome in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek at Naqsh-e Rostam
The fall of the Sasanian empire to the Arab conquerors makes Arabic the language of government
The Samanid court at Bukhara patronises poetry in the new Persian language
Ferdowsi completes the Shahnameh, the national epic of the Persian-speaking world
Death of the poet Rumi, author of the Masnavi
The Mughal emperor Akbar makes Persian the language of all government records in his empire
Persian is replaced by English and local languages as the official language of British India

f.family: Indo-European: the south-western group of the Iranian languages, a branch of Indo-Iranian
f.script: Old Persian cuneiform; Middle Persian in scripts derived from Aramaic; New Persian in the Arabic alphabet, and in Tajikistan in Cyrillic
f.earliest: The Behistun inscription of Darius I, about 520 BCE
f.status: The first language of more than 70 million people and a second language of millions more; official in Iran, in Afghanistan as Dari and in Tajikistan as Tajik
